newsitem.title: USA: USDA may lift some Karnal bunt quarantines in SW.
newsitem.headline: USDA may lift some Karnal bunt quarantines in SW.

text.p: The Agriculture Department may lift some of its Karnal bunt quarantines and other restrictions placed last year in wheat growing areas of Arizona, California and the southwest if recent tests show that the fungus infestation was not as large as first thought, a senior USDA official said Monday.

"We know there's Karnal bunt there ... we've found bunted wheat in the Southwest ... But hopefully it's not as widespread as we initially thought," said Paul Drazek, senior adviser to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman and the head of the department's team to control the spread of the fungus.

Earlier on Monday, the department announced that it would immediately lift all restrictions for Karnal bunt in the U.S. Southeast because recent tests have indicated no presence of the fungus in those areas.
What had been originally identified as Karnal bunt in the Southeast has now been correctly identified as ryegrass smut, which poses no danger to wheat, the department said.

Drazek said the department has discovered that ryegrass smut may also have been incorrectly identified as Karnal bunt in some of the quarantined southwestern areas, and that the agency will move quickly to ease restrictions in those areas.

"Where we have a similar situation in areas of the Southwest, we will be proposing regulatory action to handle the situation in a similar fashion (as the Southeast)," Drazek said. "There may be areas in Arizona and California where we may be able to make a similar determination."
Drazek said it has always been USDA's hope that the agency would be able to reduce the size of the quarantine, "and that's what we're going to do."
Discovery of the karnal bunt fungus last spring in southwestern wheat areas roiled grain markets throughout the world.

The fungus discovery caused the USDA to temporarily suspend U.S. wheat exports, quarantine large areas of Arizona and California - along with some areas in New Mexico and Texas - and forced producers to destroy wheat fields and implement other drastic measures to stop the spread of the disease.
Drazek said that given the importance of U.S. wheat exports and the potential loss of billions of dollars of commercial business, he did not think the department had over-reacted.
"The terrible disruption would have been if we had not done anything, because we would have lost exports in the billion of dollars, probably," he said.
Drazek said the department wants to act as quickly as possible, noting that farmers will soon be harvesting wheat in the Southwest.
"The harvest is approaching and we're going to make every effort to get it into place by then," Drazek said.
